note: Authored per-skill review item banks — client-scorable recognition items (source ref, stem, choices, correct index, feedback). Empty until an educator authors items in docs/item-authoring-workbench.html and imports them (npm run graph:import-items -- <export.json>). sourceReviewItems (data/curriculum-engine.mjs) prefers these over the graph-derived retrievals, so authored items upgrade a skill's reviews the moment they land. The >=3-items-per-skill bank (foundation-graph-schema.md step 10) fills here.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Read this line, then say what kind of text it is:

שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
"Hear, O Israel: the LORD is our God, the LORD is one." (Deuteronomy 6:4)

What kind of text is this?
choices: A verse of the Torah
A passage of Mishnah
A passage of Gemara
A line of commentary
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: It is a verse of the Torah — Scripture in its own voice, stated directly, with no sage's name and no question-and-answer around it.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Read this line, then say what kind of text it is:

מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּעַרְבִין
"From when may one recite the Shema in the evening?" (Mishnah Berakhot 1:1)

What kind of text is this?
choices: A passage of Mishnah
A verse of the Torah
A passage of Gemara
A line of commentary
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: It is Mishnah — a compact rule or question about practice, in tight Hebrew, that sages then dispute; not Scripture and not the Aramaic discussion that follows it.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Read this line, then say what kind of text it is:

תַּנָּא הֵיכָא קָאֵי דְּקָתָנֵי מֵאֵימָתַי
"Where does the Tanna stand [what is he discussing], that he teaches 'from when'?" (Berakhot 2a)

What kind of text is this?
choices: A passage of Gemara
A passage of Mishnah
A verse of the Torah
A line of commentary
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: It is Gemara — it questions and analyzes the Mishnah, here in Aramaic (דְּקָתָנֵי, 'that he teaches'), rather than simply stating a rule.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Read this line, then say what kind of text it is:

בְּרֵאשִׁית — אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי
"'In the beginning' — this verse says nothing other than 'interpret me.'" (Rashi on Genesis 1:1)

What kind of text is this?
choices: A line of commentary
A verse of the Torah
A passage of Mishnah
A passage of Gemara
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: It is commentary — it quotes a word from the base text (בְּרֵאשִׁית) and then explains it. That quoted-word-then-explanation shape is the tell of Rashi and other commentaries.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Two lines come from the same page:

(1) מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּעַרְבִין — "From when may one recite the Shema in the evening?"
(2) תַּנָּא הֵיכָא קָאֵי דְּקָתָנֵי מֵאֵימָתַי — "Where does the Tanna stand, that he teaches 'from when'?"

Which line is the Gemara?
choices: Line 2 — it opens a question about line 1
Line 1 — it states the opening rule of the page
Both lines are Gemara discussion here
Neither line is Gemara; both are Torah
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: Line 1 is the Mishnah (it states the opening rule); line 2 is the Gemara, which opens a question about it. The Mishnah states; the Gemara probes.

fnd-orient-source-type.stem:
Both lines mention the same opening words:

(1) בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ — "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
(2) בְּרֵאשִׁית — אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי — "'In the beginning' — this verse says nothing other than 'interpret me.'"

Which line is the commentary?
choices: Line 2 — it quotes a word, then explains it
Line 1 — it is the verse being explained here
Both lines are lines of commentary
Both lines are the plain Torah verse
fnd-orient-source-type.feedback: Line 1 is the Torah verse itself. Line 2 is commentary — it lifts a word from the verse and comments on it (the quoted-word-then-explanation shape).

fnd-orient-page-geography.stem: On a standard printed Talmud page, the block of text runs down the center and different commentaries sit in the columns around it. Which block is the primary Talmud text you are learning?
choices: The central block, which carries the Mishnah and Gemara themselves.
The inner-margin column, which is where the main text always sits.
The outer-margin column, since commentary is printed largest.
Whichever block has the most vowels printed on it.
fnd-orient-page-geography.feedback: The center column is the Mishnah and Gemara; the surrounding columns (such as Rashi and Tosafot) are commentary that frames the main text.

fnd-orient-page-geography.stem: On a Mikraot Gedolot page, a Torah verse sits at the top and several commentaries are printed beneath and around it. What is the relationship you should read first?
choices: The verse is the primary text; the surrounding material comments on it.
The longest commentary is the primary text and the verse illustrates it.
Each block is an independent source with no particular center.
The commentaries must be read before the verse can be understood at all.
fnd-orient-page-geography.feedback: The verse is the center of a Mikraot Gedolot page; the commentaries orbit it, so you orient to the verse before weighing what others say about it.

fnd-orient-page-geography.stem: Reading down a Talmud page you reach the abbreviation גמ׳. What does its position tell you about where you are?
choices: The Mishnah just ended and the Gemara's discussion of it begins here.
A brand-new tractate is starting from the top on this very line.
A Torah verse is being quoted here for the very first time.
The page is finished and the next daf begins right below.
fnd-orient-page-geography.feedback: גמ׳ marks the start of the Gemara; seeing it tells you the Mishnah is done and the analysis of it now opens.

fnd-orient-speaker.stem: A line reads, in effect, "Moshe received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on...", with no name attached to the sentence itself. Whose voice is telling you this?
choices: The anonymous voice of the Mishnah, narrating the chain of transmission.
Moshe himself, speaking about his own life in the first person.
A named later sage whose attribution formula opens the line.
God, quoted here directly and by name as the one speaking.
fnd-orient-speaker.feedback: With no attribution formula, the sentence is the Mishnah's own anonymous narrating voice, not any single named person speaking.

fnd-orient-speaker.stem: A line begins with a name followed by "used to say" and then a teaching. What does that opening tell you to do before weighing the teaching?
choices: Attach the teaching to the named sage as its speaker.
Treat the teaching as the anonymous Mishnah's own ruling.
Assume the teaching is a direct quotation of a Torah verse.
Read the name as the audience being addressed, not the speaker.
fnd-orient-speaker.feedback: An attribution formula ("Rabbi X used to say") names the speaker; identifying whose view it is comes before deciding what to make of it.

fnd-orient-speaker.stem: In a Gemara line "Rabbi Yochanan said..." is embedded inside the anonymous discussion. Who is speaking the reported statement, and who is framing it?
choices: Rabbi Yochanan is quoted; the anonymous Gemara frames and reports him.
The anonymous Gemara is speaking; Rabbi Yochanan is the one being addressed.
Rabbi Yochanan both frames the sugya and reports every other view in it.
There is no framing voice; the whole line is a single verse.
fnd-orient-speaker.feedback: The named statement is the quoted view; the surrounding anonymous voice reports and arranges it, so a line can carry a speaker inside a framer.

fnd-orient-unit-boundary.stem: A Mishnah first fixes when the evening Shema may be recited, then turns to a different dispute about how late it may be said. How should you mark these?
choices: As two units: one idea closes before the next question opens.
As one continuous idea, since they share the same tractate.
As unrelated verses that happen to be printed together.
As a single ruling followed by its own margin commentary.
fnd-orient-unit-boundary.feedback: When the topic shifts from one question to a distinct dispute, one unit of thought has ended and another begins; naming that boundary keeps the reading clear.

fnd-orient-unit-boundary.stem: Reading a Gemara, the discussion resolves one question and then a fresh question is posed on a new point. What does the fresh question mark?
choices: The start of a new unit of discussion, distinct from the one just closed.
A restatement of the very same question in slightly different words.
The end of the whole tractate, with nothing further to follow.
A quotation of a Torah verse rather than any new question at all.
fnd-orient-unit-boundary.feedback: A new question on a new point opens a new unit; recognizing where one discussion stops and the next starts is what keeps a long sugya legible.

fnd-orient-unit-boundary.stem: You are reading the opening of the Torah and reach the end of the seventh day before the text turns to a second telling of creation. Where is the unit boundary?
choices: At the close of the seventh day, where the first account completes.
In the middle of the first verse, at the first strong word.
There is no boundary; the whole book is one undivided unit.
Only at chapter numbers, which the original text itself supplies.
fnd-orient-unit-boundary.feedback: The first account closes when the seventh day is done; a unit boundary follows the shape of the idea, not the printed chapter numbers added later.

fnd-orient-question-present.stem: The Gemara opens with מאימתי ("from when...?"). Is this line asking or telling, and how do you know?
choices: Asking: the word opens an inquiry that the discussion will try to answer.
Telling: it states a settled fact that plainly needs no answer.
Neither: it is simply a name introducing the next speaker.
Telling: it is a direct quotation lifted from a Torah verse.
fnd-orient-question-present.feedback: מאימתי is a question word; noticing that the source is asking, not asserting, sets you up to look for the answer that follows.

fnd-orient-question-present.stem: A Mishnah states plainly that the evening Shema is recited from a certain hour. Is the line asking or telling?
choices: Telling: it asserts the practice as a settled rule.
Asking: it is inviting the reader to supply the hour.
Both at once: every Mishnah is a question and an answer together.
Neither: it is a margin comment, not a statement.
fnd-orient-question-present.feedback: A plain assertion of a rule is telling; distinguishing it from a question keeps you from hunting for an answer the line never asked for.

fnd-orient-question-present.stem: A Gemara line reads, in effect, "What is the source for this?" before citing a proof. Asking or telling?
choices: Asking: it demands a source, and the citation that follows is the answer.
Telling: it is simply stating the source outright and plainly.
Neither: it is naming the sage who happens to speak next.
Telling: it is the settled conclusion of the whole discussion.
fnd-orient-question-present.feedback: "What is the source?" is a question that sets up the proof; reading it as an inquiry tells you the next line is meant to answer it.

fnd-signal-known-words.stem: You keep meeting the word אָמַר as you read. What does sight-reading such a high-frequency word buy you?
choices: Attention to spare for the argument instead of re-decoding it.
A guarantee that the sentence is a question, not a statement.
Proof that the passage is quoting a verse of the Torah.
A signal that a brand-new tractate is about to begin here.
fnd-signal-known-words.feedback: Fluent recognition of common words frees working memory for the reasoning; that is the point of a word bank.

fnd-signal-known-words.stem: The word בָּרוּךְ opens many prayers and blessings. Recognizing it instantly helps you because you can...?
choices: Expect a blessing formula and read for whom it praises.
Assume the text is a legal ruling that must be decided.
Know that a named sage is about to be quoted next.
Skip the rest of the line as unimportant filler.
fnd-signal-known-words.feedback: High-frequency openers set your expectation for the genre that follows; בָּרוּךְ flags a blessing.

fnd-signal-known-words.stem: A reader who must stop and decode every common word will most likely...?
choices: Lose the thread of the passage while decoding each word.
Understand the argument better than a fluent reader would.
Finish the passage faster than a fluent reader would.
Correctly identify every rare word before the common ones.
fnd-signal-known-words.feedback: Stopping on common words breaks comprehension; a rehearsed word bank keeps the thread intact.

fnd-signal-question-words.stem: The sugya opens with מַאי ("what?"). What kind of answer does this question word invite?
choices: An explanation or definition of the term in question.
A named sage to whom the line is being attributed.
A blessing formula offering praise to God.
A count of how many separate cases follow.
fnd-signal-question-words.feedback: מַאי asks for an explanation or definition; matching a question word to its expected answer sets up the reading.

fnd-signal-question-words.stem: You see מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵי ("from where do we know these things?"). What should you expect next?
choices: A cited source brought as proof for the rule.
A plain restatement of the very same rule.
A change of speaker to a different sage.
The conclusion that ends the whole discussion.
fnd-signal-question-words.feedback: מנא הני מילי asks for a source; the next line typically supplies a proof text.

fnd-signal-question-words.stem: Recognizing a question word before reading the rest of a line mainly lets you...?
choices: Predict the shape of the answer and read toward it.
Skip the answer, since the question alone suffices.
Assume the line is quoting some other source.
Decide the practical halakhah on the spot.
fnd-signal-question-words.feedback: A question word primes you for the kind of answer coming, so you read with a purpose.

fnd-signal-name-formulas.stem: A line reads רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר ("Rabbi Eliezer says"). What does this formula do?
choices: Hands the words that follow to Rabbi Eliezer as his view.
Signals that the previous ruling is now being overturned.
Marks the beginning of a quoted verse from the Torah.
Brings the current unit of discussion to its close.
fnd-signal-name-formulas.feedback: An attribution formula assigns the following words to a named voice; here they are Rabbi Eliezer's.

fnd-signal-name-formulas.stem: You meet אָמַר רַב ("Rav said") embedded in the discussion. To read accurately you should...?
choices: Attach the statement that follows to Rav as its speaker.
Treat the words that follow as the Gemara's own voice.
Read it as a question that is awaiting an answer.
Assume a verse of Torah is now being cited.
fnd-signal-name-formulas.feedback: "Amar Rav" attributes the next words to Rav; tracking who speaks keeps the voices straight.

fnd-signal-name-formulas.stem: Why is it worth marking every attribution formula in a passage?
choices: So you can list the voices and see who disagrees with whom.
So you can safely skip whatever a named sage says.
So you can tell prose sections apart from poetry.
So you can count how many verses are quoted.
fnd-signal-name-formulas.feedback: Attributions let you map the conversation of voices, which is where the disagreement lives.

fnd-signal-connectors.stem: A line hinges on the connector אֶלָּא ("rather"). What move does it signal?
choices: A correction that replaces the prior explanation.
An added example supporting the prior point.
A citation of a proof text from Scripture.
A plain restatement of the same claim.
fnd-signal-connectors.feedback: אלא marks a corrective turn; the text is rejecting what came before and substituting a new reading.

fnd-signal-connectors.stem: You meet שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ("as it says"). What kind of connector is this?
choices: A citing connector introducing a proof text.
An opposing connector raising an objection.
An adding connector piling on another case.
A concluding connector stating the ruling.
fnd-signal-connectors.feedback: שנאמר introduces a citation; sorting connectors into adding, opposing, or citing reveals the argument's shape.

fnd-signal-connectors.stem: Reading only the connectors of a passage first helps you...?
choices: Feel the shape of the argument before the details.
Memorize the full vocabulary of the passage.
Identify exactly who each of the speakers is.
Decide the practical halakhah of the passage.
fnd-signal-connectors.feedback: Connectors carry the logical skeleton; skimming them previews how the argument moves.

fnd-signal-quotation.stem: After דִּכְתִיב ("as it is written") comes a run of words from Tanakh. How should you treat them?
choices: As borrowed words quoted from another text.
As the Gemara's own newly-made claim.
As a question being posed to the reader.
As an attribution to some named sage.
fnd-signal-quotation.feedback: A citation formula marks the next words as borrowed; bracket them as quoted, not the source's own voice.

fnd-signal-quotation.stem: A passage on honoring parents strings together several verses. Recognizing the citations lets you...?
choices: Separate the quoted verses from the argument built on them.
Assume every verse cited says exactly the same thing.
Skip past the verses as mere decoration.
Treat the sage as the author of the verses.
fnd-signal-quotation.feedback: Bracketing quoted verses keeps them distinct from the reasoning that uses them.

fnd-signal-quotation.stem: Which is the clearest sign that a source is quoting another text rather than speaking for itself?
choices: A citation formula such as "as it is written" precedes the words.
The quoted words are printed in a noticeably larger font.
The passage in question is unusually short overall.
A named sage appears somewhere else on the page.
fnd-signal-quotation.feedback: Citation formulas, not layout, are the reliable signal that borrowed words follow.

fnd-role-question-vs-answer.stem: A line asks when the Shema is read; the next line names a time. How do you label the two lines?
choices: The first is a question, the second is its answer.
Both lines are answers to an unstated question.
The first is a ruling, the second a citation.
Both lines merely restate the Mishnah's words.
fnd-role-question-vs-answer.feedback: Tagging lines as question, answer, or restatement turns a passage into a legible chain.

fnd-role-question-vs-answer.stem: A line repeats the previous point in different words without adding anything. What is its role?
choices: A restatement of what was already said.
A fresh objection raised against the claim.
A proof text drawn from the Tanakh.
A new question opening a new topic.
fnd-role-question-vs-answer.feedback: Not every line advances the argument; a restatement re-says the prior point and should be tagged R.

fnd-role-question-vs-answer.stem: God answers Job with a long series of questions. In a question-and-answer tagging, these lines are...?
choices: Questions, even though no plain answer follows them.
Answers, because they conclude the book's argument.
Restatements of Job's own earlier complaint.
Citations of a source outside the book.
fnd-role-question-vs-answer.feedback: A line's role is its form: these are questions by shape, whether or not a tidy answer follows.

fnd-role-example.stem: After stating a rule about damages, the Mishnah turns to "an ox that gored...". What is that turn?
choices: A worked example testing the rule just stated.
A new and entirely unrelated rule.
A quotation brought from the Torah.
The final ruling of the whole tractate.
fnd-role-example.feedback: When a text drops into a concrete case, read it as a test of the rule it follows.

fnd-role-example.stem: A mussar work names a trait, then describes "someone who..." in a specific situation. The specific case is...?
choices: An example showing the trait in action.
A digression unrelated to the trait.
A legal ruling about the person described.
A quotation of some earlier sage.
fnd-role-example.feedback: "Someone who..." usually introduces an example that makes an abstract trait concrete.

fnd-role-example.stem: Why does recognizing an example matter for understanding the rule?
choices: The example shows the rule's boundaries in a real case.
The example simply replaces the rule entirely.
The example is there only to add length.
The example proves the rule must be wrong.
fnd-role-example.feedback: Examples test and bound a rule; naming which rule an example serves is the reading move.

fnd-role-quotation-bounds.stem: A teaching cites a verse and then comments on it. To read it well you must...?
choices: Mark where the quoted verse ends and the comment begins.
Treat the whole line as a single continuous quotation.
Assume the comment is also drawn from the Tanakh.
Ignore the verse and read only the comment.
fnd-role-quotation-bounds.feedback: Bounding a quotation keeps the cited words apart from the voice interpreting them.

fnd-role-quotation-bounds.stem: The Gemara quotes part of a verse, then returns to its own argument. The risk if you miss that boundary is...?
choices: Reading the Gemara's own words as if Scripture said them.
Finding the passage too short to follow at all.
Mistaking the speaker for Rabbi Akiva.
Skipping the ruling that comes at the end.
fnd-role-quotation-bounds.feedback: If you don't mark where the quote ends, you attribute the source's own reasoning to the verse.

fnd-role-quotation-bounds.stem: A code cites an earlier authority mid-sentence. Bounding the quotation means...?
choices: Separating the cited words from the code's own ruling.
Deciding that the quotation is the final law.
Treating the entire sentence as one single voice.
Discarding the citation as irrelevant to the law.
fnd-role-quotation-bounds.feedback: Marking the cited words apart from the citing voice is what keeps the two straight.

fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.stem: A line states plainly what a person should do, closing off the alternatives. Is this ruling or discussion?
choices: A ruling, because it decides and closes options.
A discussion, because it explores possibilities.
A quotation with no position of its own.
A question that is still awaiting an answer.
fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.feedback: A decision that closes options is a ruling; the deciding word is the tell.

fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.stem: A passage weighs two views and says "these and those are the words of the living God" (אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ). This is...?
choices: Discussion that holds both views open.
A ruling that decides firmly between them.
A citation of a single Torah verse.
A restatement of one earlier line.
fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.feedback: Elu va-elu keeps both readings alive; it explores rather than decides, so it is discussion.

fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.stem: What is the quickest way to tell a ruling from a discussion?
choices: Ask whether the text decides or keeps options open.
Count how many separate sages are named.
Check whether Hebrew or Aramaic is used.
Measure how long the passage happens to be.
fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion.feedback: Decides means ruling, explores means discussion; that question is the discriminator.

fnd-case-actors.stem: Two people are holding a garment, each claiming it. Who are the actors you should list first?
choices: The two claimants, each asserting that it is his.
Only the court and its scribes on the scene.
The Torah and the Mishnah as the speakers.
A single owner together with one witness.
fnd-case-actors.feedback: Naming the cast of actors and what each does is the first step in mapping a case.

fnd-case-actors.stem: In the binding of Isaac, listing the actors and their actions means noting that...?
choices: Abraham journeys and binds, Isaac is bound, the angel calls out.
Only Abraham matters, since he is the main figure.
The narrator alone acts, since he tells the story.
God acts but no human participant does anything.
fnd-case-actors.feedback: A case's actors are everyone who acts; attach one verb to each to see the situation.

fnd-case-actors.stem: Why identify who acts before asking the legal question?
choices: The rights at stake depend on who did what.
The actors never actually affect the ruling.
It lets you skip reading the case itself.
It tells you which tractate you are in.
fnd-case-actors.feedback: Who acts and how frames the whole case; the legal question rides on it.

fnd-case-what-happens.stem: Before analyzing liability, what should you be able to say about a damages case?
choices: A one-sentence plain account of what happened.
The final ruling and its Torah source.
Every sage who has ever discussed it.
The Aramaic term for each action taken.
fnd-case-what-happens.feedback: Tell the case as a plain one-sentence story before touching the legal question.

fnd-case-what-happens.stem: For the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, stating "what happens" plainly means saying that...?
choices: A man is shamed at a feast after a mistaken invitation.
A ruling about invitations is finally decided.
A verse of the Torah is being expounded here.
An argument between two named sages is traced.
fnd-case-what-happens.feedback: Plain-language retelling captures the situation before any lesson is drawn from it.

fnd-case-what-happens.stem: What is the danger of skipping the plain-language summary of a case?
choices: Arguing the law while still unclear on what happened.
Understanding the case far too quickly.
Finishing the passage far too slowly.
Naming rather too many of the actors.
fnd-case-what-happens.feedback: Legal analysis built on a fuzzy grasp of the facts goes wrong; state the facts first.

fnd-case-restate.stem: You close the text, retell the case, then reopen it. What are you checking?
choices: Which details you dropped or changed in the retelling.
Whether the ruling of the case is ultimately correct.
Who printed the particular edition you are reading.
How many separate verses the passage happens to quote.
fnd-case-restate.feedback: Restating from memory then checking against the text exposes what you truly grasped.

fnd-case-restate.stem: A faithful restatement in your own words should...?
choices: Preserve the case accurately without copying its wording.
Quote the original sentence exactly word for word.
Add a fresh ruling of your own to the case.
Leave out the case's main action entirely.
fnd-case-restate.feedback: Restating tests understanding: keep the substance, drop the reliance on the exact words.

fnd-case-restate.stem: Retelling a case in your own words mainly builds...?
choices: Real understanding rather than surface familiarity.
A larger vocabulary of rare Hebrew words.
Greater speed at decoding the letters.
Knowledge of how the page is laid out.
fnd-case-restate.feedback: Owning a case in your own words is the difference between understanding and mere recognition.

fnd-case-uncertainty.stem: The Mishnah asks until when the evening Shema may be recited, and the views differ. The uncertainty is...?
choices: The cutoff time that the case turns on.
Whether the Shema exists as a text at all.
Who the author of the Mishnah was.
Which language the Mishnah is written in.
fnd-case-uncertainty.feedback: The open question is what the case needs settled; here it is the latest permitted time.

fnd-case-uncertainty.stem: Two people claim a found garment and neither can prove ownership. Naming the uncertainty means...?
choices: Stating that ownership cannot be established from these facts.
Deciding at once in favor of whichever party spoke first.
Noting merely that the garment is a valuable object.
Listing the tractate and chapter in which it appears.
fnd-case-uncertainty.feedback: The uncertainty is the missing thing needed to decide: here, proof of who owns the garment.

fnd-case-uncertainty.stem: How do you locate the point of uncertainty in a case?
choices: Ask what the case would need in order to be decided.
Count how many actors are involved in it.
Find the single longest sentence in it.
Identify the earliest sage it names.
fnd-case-uncertainty.feedback: The missing piece required for a decision is the uncertainty the case turns on.

fnd-arg-claim.stem: Rambam opens by asserting a First Being who brings all else into existence. Stated as a claim, this is...?
choices: "There is a First Cause on whom all else depends."
A question about who first created the world.
A citation of a verse offered without comment.
An objection raised against an earlier view.
fnd-arg-claim.feedback: State the claim in one sentence ('This source claims that...') before analyzing anything else.

fnd-arg-claim.stem: To find a passage's claim, the most useful first move is to finish which sentence?
choices: "This source claims that..."
"The rarest word on the page is..."
"The name of the speaker here is..."
"The number printed on this page is..."
fnd-arg-claim.feedback: Naming the claim first orients everything else you notice in the passage.

fnd-arg-claim.stem: Which of these is a claim, as opposed to some other kind of line?
choices: "Everything depends on God for its existence."
"From where do we learn this teaching?"
"As it is written in the Torah..."
"Rabbi Yehuda says the following:"
fnd-arg-claim.feedback: A claim asserts something; questions, citations, and attributions are other roles, not claims.

fnd-arg-evidence-role.stem: A verse is brought that directly backs the stated rule. What job is that citation doing?
choices: Supporting the claim as a proof.
Attacking the claim as a counterexample.
Refining the claim's precise scope.
Splitting the claim into two cases.
fnd-arg-evidence-role.feedback: Ask of each citation: does it prop, attack, refine, or split? Here it props the claim.

fnd-arg-evidence-role.stem: Two verses on honoring parents are compared to show they cover different things. The second verse's role is to...?
choices: Refine the claim by distinguishing what each verse covers.
Simply repeat the first verse's point again.
Reject the whole idea of honoring parents.
End the discussion with a final ruling.
fnd-arg-evidence-role.feedback: A citation that draws a distinction is refining, not merely supporting.

fnd-arg-evidence-role.stem: Why name the job a cited source is doing rather than just noting that it appears?
choices: The same verse can support, challenge, or refine a claim.
Citations never change how the argument actually works.
It tells you who printed the edition you are holding.
It makes the passage noticeably shorter to read through.
fnd-arg-evidence-role.feedback: A citation's force depends on its job; identifying prop/attack/refine/split is the reading move.

fnd-arg-objection.stem: The Gemara raises a case that the stated rule seems to get wrong. What is this move?
choices: An objection pressing on the rule.
A proof brought to support the rule.
A restatement of the rule itself.
An attribution of the rule to a sage.
fnd-arg-objection.feedback: An objection pushes back; name what it threatens — the claim, its reason, or its scope.

fnd-arg-objection.stem: When you mark an objection, the key thing to describe is...?
choices: Exactly what pressure it puts on the claim.
How many words it happens to contain.
Which typeface it is printed in.
Whether its phrasing happens to rhyme.
fnd-arg-objection.feedback: An objection matters by what it endangers; say whether it hits the claim, its reason, or its reach.

fnd-arg-objection.stem: A text anticipates a reader's difficulty and states it plainly before answering. That stated difficulty is...?
choices: An objection the author raises in order to address it.
The author's own final conclusion on the matter.
A quotation lifted from an opponent's book.
An abrupt change to a different topic.
fnd-arg-objection.feedback: Authors often voice an objection themselves; recognizing it as an objection sets up the response.

fnd-arg-response.stem: After an objection, the Gemara limits the rule to a narrower case. How does the response work?
choices: It narrows the claim so the objection no longer applies.
It denies that any objection was ever raised.
It abandons the original claim entirely.
It merely repeats the objection in other words.
fnd-arg-response.feedback: Ask whether a response denies, limits, or accepts-and-adjusts; here it narrows the claim.

fnd-arg-response.stem: A response that grants an objection's point but adjusts the original claim is doing what?
choices: Accepting and reframing rather than flatly denying.
Ignoring the objection completely.
Restating the objection as its own view.
Citing a verse with no comment at all.
fnd-arg-response.feedback: Responses aren't only denials; naming deny/limit/adjust tells you how the argument moved.

fnd-arg-response.stem: To follow a response well, the question to ask is...?
choices: Does it deny the objection, limit it, or adjust the claim?
How many named sages are mentioned within the response?
Is the response itself written in Hebrew or in Aramaic?
Where exactly does the response sit on the printed page?
fnd-arg-response.feedback: Classifying the response as deny/limit/adjust is how you track the argument's resolution.

fnd-arg-unresolved.stem: The Oven of Akhnai story ends without the tension between the voices tidily settled. Recognizing this means...?
choices: Naming the tension the passage deliberately leaves open.
Assuming a ruling was simply omitted by mistake.
Treating the last speaker as the decided law.
Concluding the passage is really about ovens.
fnd-arg-unresolved.feedback: Some passages leave a tension standing on purpose; noticing the openness is itself the reading.

fnd-arg-unresolved.stem: Job's ending restores his fortunes but leaves the deeper question of suffering not fully answered. This openness...?
choices: May be the point, not a defect in the text.
Proves the book was simply left unfinished.
Means the question was already answered earlier.
Shows the text is quoting another book.
fnd-arg-unresolved.feedback: Ask whether an unresolved ending is intentional; in Job the open question does real work.

fnd-arg-unresolved.stem: How do you tell a deliberately open ending from a resolved one?
choices: Check whether the passage decides, and if not, name what stands open.
Count how many separate verses the passage happens to cite.
See whether the passage runs longer than a single page.
Find the earliest named sage the passage happens to mention.
fnd-arg-unresolved.feedback: First ask if it resolves; if it doesn't, naming the standing tension is the move.

fnd-context-genre-expectations.stem: You are reading a psalm that pours out trust in God through images of a shepherd and still waters. What is fair to ask of this text, and what is not?
choices: Ask it for resonance and imagery, not for a precise legal ruling.
Ask it for a precise legal ruling on how to pray.
Ask it to settle a dispute between two named sages.
Ask it for the exact clock times of daily prayer.
fnd-context-genre-expectations.feedback: A psalm is poetry: it offers resonance and imagery. Demanding a precise legal ruling from it mistakes what the genre can deliver.

fnd-context-genre-expectations.sourceRef: One passage with a ruling and a story side by side
fnd-context-genre-expectations.stem: In one passage you find two things side by side: a legal ruling about what to do, and a story about a sage's life. Reading with genre in mind, how should your expectations differ?
choices: Read the ruling for precise practice; read the story for meaning, not binding law.
Read both of them as equally binding legal rulings to follow.
Read both only as stories, with no practical weight at all.
Ignore the story entirely, since only the ruling could matter.
fnd-context-genre-expectations.feedback: The law-and-practice side is called halakhah; it invites precise practice. The story-and-meaning side is called aggadah; it invites meaning and character. Matching your stance to each is the genre move.

fnd-context-genre-expectations.stem: A legal code states, in plain terms, exactly what to do in a situation. What does this genre invite — and not invite?
choices: Precision about the rule, not a poem's open-ended resonance.
Emotional resonance far above precise practical detail.
A single correct feeling the reader is meant to have.
A narrative about how the law was first handed down.
fnd-context-genre-expectations.feedback: A code invites precision; a poem invites resonance. Reading a code like a poem — or a poem like a code — misreads the genre.

fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.sourceRef: A source with several undecided views
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.stem: You study a source that lays out several different views and does not decide between them. What have you gained, and what have you not gained?
choices: You learned the range of views, not a ruling for your own practice.
You received a binding ruling to follow right away.
You learned nothing at all until a teacher rules on it.
You must simply follow whichever view happens to appear first.
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.feedback: Studying the views teaches you what the source says; it does not by itself tell you what to do. That step needs more than reading — often asking a knowledgeable teacher.

fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.sourceRef: A code of Jewish law with disagreeing explanations
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.stem: You read a code of Jewish law where later explanations disagree about how to apply it. Studying this on your own, what is the responsible thing to say about your own practice?
choices: I understand the disagreement; deciding what to do needs a knowledgeable teacher.
I can now confidently rule for myself and for other people.
The first explanation I happened to read is binding on me.
Because the explanations disagree, none of it applies to anyone.
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.feedback: Learning a disagreement is not the same as being told what to do. Naming the limit — 'I have learned, but not yet been told what to do' — is the responsible move.

fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.sourceRef: A source of Jewish law studied on your own
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.stem: What is the honest way to state where you stand after studying a source of Jewish law on your own?
choices: "I have learned what the source says, not yet what to do."
"I have been given a ruling I must act on right now."
"I have learned nothing here that is worth knowing."
"My own reading overrides what any teacher would say."
fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling.feedback: The responsible boundary: study yields understanding, not a personal ruling. Say what you have learned and what you have not yet been told to do.
